pages.x: In the 1100s two warrior clans rose to power in Japan: the Taira, with red banners, and the Minamoto, with white. In 1160 the Taira leader, Kiyomori, beat the Minamoto and came to rule the court at Kyoto. In 1180 he made his grandson Antoku, aged one, emperor.

Kiyomori had spared the young sons of the Minamoto leader he killed, sending them to temples and into exile. In 1180 one of them, Yoritomo, now grown, raised the white banners in the east, and the war began. Kiyomori died of a fever the next year.

Yoritomo's young half-brother Yoshitsune became the war's hero. At Ichi-no-Tani in 1184 he led horsemen down a slope so steep no one thought it could be ridden, and fell on the Taira camp from behind.

In 1185 the last battle was fought at sea, in the strait of Dan-no-ura. When the tide turned against the Taira, Kiyomori's widow took the boy emperor Antoku, aged six, in her arms and leapt into the sea with him. Most of the Taira lords drowned.

Fishermen near Dan-no-ura say that the Heike crabs, whose shells look like the angry faces of samurai, carry the spirits of the drowned Taira warriors. The astronomer Carl Sagan used them to explain how selection can shape living things.

Yoritomo did not trust his famous brother and hunted him to his death in 1189. In 1192 the emperor named Yoritomo shogun, the chief general. From Kamakura he ruled Japan, while the emperors in Kyoto kept their titles and ceremonies.
Blind monks with lutes sang the story of the war for generations before it was written down. It begins with the sound of temple bells, telling that all things pass and the proud do not last.

The Genpei War put samurai in charge of Japan for nearly 700 years, under shoguns who ruled in the emperor's name, until 1868. Its heroes and its sad ending, above all the doomed Yoshitsune, became favourite stories of Japanese theatre.
pts: A boy emperor drowned at Dan-no-ura
Began 700 years of rule by shoguns
